n: The Song of Moses opens like a court case: heaven and earth are called as witnesses to hear the testimony. This is Hebrew poetry, with paired lines that echo each other.
Moses hopes his teaching will refresh like gentle rain and dew on young plants — nourishing, not crushing.

f.w: My doctrine shall drop as the rain

n: The song’s purpose: to proclaim the name of the Lord and invite all to praise his greatness.

f.w: publish the name of the LORD

n: God is “the Rock” — stable, unchanging, a refuge. His work is flawless and his ways are just. Paul and the Book of Mormon identify this Rock with Christ.
In contrast, Israel has corrupted itself. Their moral defects show they are not acting like God’s children.

f.w: their spot is not the spot of his children
f.g: Their blemish shows they are not truly his children; the Hebrew is difficult.

n: Is this how you repay the Lord? He is your Father, who bought and created you. Ingratitude toward such a parent is foolishness.

f.w: is not he thy father that hath bought thee

n: Remember history — ask your parents and grandparents. Family memory carries the story of God’s goodness.

f.w: ask thy father, and he will shew thee

n: When God divided the nations at Babel, he set their boundaries with Israel in mind. (A Dead Sea Scroll reads “sons of God” here instead of “children of Israel.”)

f.g: Hebrew Elyon, a title for God.

f.w: he set the bounds of the people

n: Out of all the nations, the Lord chose Israel as his own special portion.

f.w: Jacob is the lot of his inheritance

n: God found Israel like a lost wanderer in a desolate desert, led and taught them, and guarded them as carefully as one guards the pupil of the eye.

f.g: The pupil — the most protected part of the eye.

n: Like a mother eagle stirring up the nest, hovering over her young, and catching them on her wings as they learn to fly.

f.w: As an eagle stirreth up her nest

n: The Lord alone led Israel — no foreign god helped. So no foreign god deserves their worship.

f.w: there was no strange god with him

n: God brought them to the heights and fed them richly. Honey and oil from rock suggest abundance even in unlikely places.

f.w: to suck honey out of the rock

n: A feast of the land’s richest foods. Wine is poetically called “the blood of the grape.”

f.g: A fertile region east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for fine livestock.

f.w: the fat of kidneys of wheat
the pure blood of the grape

n: “Jeshurun” (“upright one”), a pet name for Israel, grew fat and kicked like a spoiled ox. Prosperity led them to forget their Maker — a pattern the Book of Mormon calls the pride cycle.

f.g: A poetic name for Israel meaning “the upright one.”

f.w: lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation

n: Their idolatry provoked God’s jealous love — his insistence on an exclusive covenant.
They sacrificed to demons — new, unknown gods with no history of saving them.

f.g: Hebrew shedim — demons or false spirits.

n: They forgot the Rock who gave them birth. God is pictured as both father and mother.

f.g: Begat = fathered; the next line uses an image of giving birth.

n: God saw and rejected them because his own sons and daughters provoked him.
God says he will hide his face and see how they end. They are a perverse, faithless generation.

f.w: children in whom is no faith

n: A fitting response: they made God jealous with “no-gods,” so he would make them jealous with a “no-people.” Paul saw this fulfilled in the Gentiles accepting the gospel.

f.w: I will move them to jealousy with those which are not a people

n: God’s anger is pictured as a fire reaching to the depths and burning the foundations of the mountains.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the deepest underworld, the realm of the dead.

n: God would pile calamities on them and shoot all his arrows — a picture of disasters as divine weapons.
Famine, plague, wild animals, and snakes would ravage them.
War outside and terror inside would strike every age — youths, young women, infants, and the elderly.

f.w: The sword without, and terror within

n: God says he could have wiped them out completely, erasing their memory.

f.g: Possibly “I will cut them to pieces.”

n: But he held back so enemies wouldn’t boast that their own strength had done it. God’s restraint protects his name.
Israel — or perhaps its enemies — lacks wisdom and understanding.
A deep sigh: if only they were wise enough to consider where their path leads!
How could one enemy chase a thousand Israelites unless God had handed Israel over? Normally God’s people should put enemies to flight.

f.w: How should one chase a thousand

n: Even Israel’s enemies admit their gods are nothing like Israel’s Rock.
The enemies’ “vine” grows from Sodom’s soil — their deeds produce poisonous, bitter fruit.
Their wine is like serpent venom.
God keeps a record of their deeds stored and sealed until the time of judgment.
Vengeance belongs to God, not to us. Their fall will come at the right time. Paul quotes this to teach Christians to leave judgment to God.

f.w: To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence

n: God will vindicate his people and have compassion when he sees their strength gone and none remaining.

f.g: Have compassion on them; God “repenting” means changing his course of action.
No one remaining, slave or free.

n: Then God will ask: Where are their gods now?
Let those gods who ate your sacrifices come and rescue you! The irony exposes idols as powerless.

f.g: Wine poured out as an offering.

n: A climactic declaration: “I, even I, am he.” God alone holds life and death, wounding and healing. Jesus’ “I am” sayings echo this language.

f.w: I kill, and I make alive

n: God swears an oath by his own eternal life, raising his hand to heaven.

f.w: I lift up my hand to heaven
f.g: The gesture of swearing an oath.

n: God as a divine warrior sharpens his flashing sword to bring justice on his enemies.
Vivid battle imagery of total victory over his foes.

f.w: from the beginning of revenges upon the enemy
f.g: Possibly “from the long-haired heads of the enemy”; the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: The song ends in hope: the nations are invited to rejoice with God’s people, for he will avenge them and cleanse his land. Paul and Hebrews quote versions of this line.

f.w: Rejoice, O ye nations, with his people
will be merciful unto his land

n: Moses, together with Joshua, recited the whole song to the people.
Moses finished speaking to Israel.
Take all of this to heart, and teach your children to obey it.

f.w: Set your hearts unto all the words

n: God’s word is not empty or trivial — it is life itself and the key to long life in the land.

f.w: it is not a vain thing for you; because it is your life

n: That same day, the Lord spoke to Moses with his final instructions.
Climb Mount Nebo in the Abarim range across from Jericho and look over the promised land.

f.g: A peak east of the north end of the Dead Sea, overlooking the Jordan valley.

n: Moses would die there and “be gathered to his people,” as Aaron had on Mount Hor. Latter-day Saint scripture adds that Moses was taken up by the Lord.

f.g: A phrase for joining one’s ancestors in death.

f.w: Aaron thy brother died in mount Hor

n: The reason: at Meribah, Moses and Aaron failed to honor God as holy before the people when water came from the rock.

f.g: You did not treat me as holy.

n: Moses will see the land from afar but not enter it — a painful yet gracious ending.

f.w: thou shalt see the land before thee
